source.title: Spurious Valleys in One-hidden-layer Neural Network Optimization Landscapes
source.authors: Luca Venturi; A. Bandeira; Joan Bruna

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes how width and activation/data conditions affect spurious valleys in one-hidden-layer networks. Its results bear conceptually on V2, but it does not run the teacher-student gradient-descent experiments or measure spurious-minimum frequency described there.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical results about spurious valleys and descent paths, not benchmark training error or empirical gradient-descent outcomes. Cited results from other work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study proves properties of spurious valleys and existence of non-increasing paths, rather than gradient-descent outcomes in realizable ReLU teacher-student problems. These related landscape properties do not establish V2's frequency of convergence to spurious minima or the benefit of adding one or two neurons. Section 6 explicitly states that the positive landscape results do not guarantee convergence of local descent algorithms. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, but its final sentence needs qualification. Finite intrinsic dimension and sufficient width rule out spurious valleys; eligible non-polynomial activations admit arbitrarily bad valleys for some distribution at every finite width. Under the random-feature assumptions, a non-increasing path from random initialization reaches loss increasingly close to irreducible risk with high probability. This does not establish gradient-descent convergence or confinement of every valley to low loss.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives theoretical landscape results for one-hidden-layer networks and selected linear networks; it does not reproduce the teacher-student gradient-descent experiments described in V2.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on activation class, data distribution (including adversarially constructed distributions), loss, width relative to intrinsic dimension or sample count, and the random-features initialization assumptions in Theorem 16.

fits_no_version.finding: Sufficient width relative to finite intrinsic dimension or sample count eliminates spurious valleys; linear and quadratic networks admit stronger sufficient-width results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated activation, loss, and width assumptions, network parameters admit non-increasing paths to global optima.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed distributions yield arbitrarily bad spurious valleys below the lower-intrinsic-dimension threshold; eligible non-polynomial activations permit such constructions at every finite width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width alone does not uniformly eliminate spurious valleys across all data distributions for the specified activation classes.

fits_no_version.finding: Under random-feature assumptions, increasing width gives high-probability existence of non-increasing paths to loss approaching the irreducible-risk baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-feature initialization permits access to increasingly low loss along some non-increasing path, without guaranteeing that gradient descent follows it.

record.problems: The results characterize loss landscapes and descent paths, not convergence of gradient descent. Negative examples use constructed worst-case distributions. Theorem 16 applies under specific random-features assumptions, and the paper identifies a gap between its high-overparameterization regime and practical regimes.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results bearing on V2 beyond the theorem and corollary statements extracted above. Cited results from prior studies and proof details that do not report separate outcomes were excluded.

untested.parts: All: convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR, label corruption, and training-recipe qualifications.
All: realizable ReLU teacher-student gradient descent from standard initialization, failure frequencies as teacher and student grow together, and adding one or two student neurons within widths 6–20.
All: depth-dependent training error in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity shortcuts, and the specified initialization exceptions.
All: initialization-dependent training speed, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
All: learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature adaptation, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
All: batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical rows can remain as related findings, but their states cannot be interpreted as observations of any supplied claim version. Remove the record's V2 support and scope-limit verdicts.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NN Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 8 establishes absence of spurious valleys above the finite upper intrinsic-dimension width threshold.

conditions.value: continuous σ; X has finite upper intrinsic dimension

rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.value: no spurious valleys for p ≥ dim*(σ, X)
rows.note: Theorem-level result for a one-hidden-layer model; it establishes existence of non-increasing paths to an optimum, not behavior of a specified gradient-descent algorithm.
rows.check: Theorem 8 establishes absence of spurious valleys at sufficient width, not gradient-descent convergence or spurious-minimum frequency under V2.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NN Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 9 establishes absence of spurious valleys for empirical risk minimization above the sample-count width threshold.
rows.measure: presence or absence of spurious valleys
rows.value: no spurious valleys for p ≥ N
rows.note: This is an ERM landscape statement, not a measured training result.
rows.check: Corollary 9 concerns ERM landscape topology at width at least the sample count. It does not measure V2's teacher-student training outcomes.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NN Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 13 constructs a data distribution that produces arbitrarily bad spurious valleys below the stated lower-intrinsic-dimension threshold.

conditions.value: non-negative σ with stated square-integrability condition

rows.measure: loss gap and intervening barrier for a spurious valley
rows.value: for any given M > 0, an open set has loss at least M above the global minimum and every path from it to a global minimum must up-climb at least M/2
rows.note: This is an existence result for a constructed distribution, not a frequency estimate across training runs.
rows.check: The constructed distributions establish arbitrarily bad valleys, without establishing V2's realizable teacher-student conditions, initialization-specific failure frequency, or response to adding neurons.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NN Φ(x; θ) = Uσ(Wx)
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 15 establishes existence of arbitrarily bad spurious valleys for some data distribution at any width.

conditions.value: continuous, non-negative, non-polynomial σ satisfying stated square-integrability condition

rows.measure: presence of arbitrarily bad spurious valleys
rows.value: such valleys exist for any hidden width p ≥ 1
rows.note: The result is worst-case over data distributions.
rows.check: For each width, some distribution produces bad valleys. This does not compare student widths for a fixed teacher problem or contradict V2's tested width benefit.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer NN Φ(x; θ) = uTσ(Wx)
rows.size_stated: width p subject to stated bounds
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 16 bounds the loss reachable by a non-increasing path from random features initialization with high probability.

conditions.value: first-layer weights sampled i.i.d. uniformly on the unit sphere
stated random-feature representation; part 2 additionally assumes sufficient regularity

rows.measure: loss at the endpoint of a non-increasing path from initialization
rows.value: part 1: at most R(X, Y) + λ if p ≥ O(λ⁻¹ log(λδ)) with probability at least 1−δ; part 2: at most R(X, Y) + O(p⁻¹+δ) with probability at least 1−e⁻O(p^δ)
rows.note: The result bounds accessible loss and discusses avoiding large barriers; it does not report a rate of spurious local minima or gradient-descent training outcomes.
rows.check: An accessible low-loss path does not establish gradient-descent success. The first width bound omits a minus sign: O(-λ⁻¹ log(λδ)). Theorem 16 samples augmented weights including biases on S^n; its setup also assumes positively homogeneous activation and the stated target representation.
